title: Experimental Design and Blocking
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter covers the statistical principles of experimental design in quantitative proteomics, focusing on the distinction between experimental and observational units, the necessity of biological replication, and the design principles of blocking and randomization. We examine how complete block designs avoid confounding and evaluate how these designs apply to experimental studies such as T-cell subsets and multi-region heart proteomes. ## Experimental Units versus Observational Units In quantitative proteomics, valid statistical inference requires distinguishing between two levels of measurement: 1. **Experimental units**: The physical entities (subjects, animals, cell cultures, or patients) to which a treatment or condition is independently applied. These represent true biological replicates. 2. **Observational units**: The entities on which individual measurements are taken. In shotgun LC-MS/MS proteomics, these are individual peptide intensity measurements. For a given protein, a single biological sample yields multiple peptide intensity measurements. These repeated peptide readings constitute technical replicates (or pseudo-replicates). While having many observational units per experimental unit permits precise estimation of technical measurement error within a sample, it does not increase the sample size for assessing population variability. Generalizing findings to a wider biological population depends strictly on the number of experimental units (biological replicates). When experimental units are limited (for instance, $n = 3$ wild-type versus $n = 3$ knockout samples), statistical power to detect treatment effects remains constrained regardless of how many peptides are measured per protein. Experiments should be designed upfront to maximize biological repeats, using a minimum of three per condition, and preferably more. ## Randomized Complete Block Designs Proteomics experiments frequently encounter technical batch effects caused by running samples across multiple days, utilizing different HPLC columns or mass spectrometers, or processing samples in separate laboratories or cell culture batches. To mitigate unwanted technical variation, experiments employ **blocking**. In a **randomized complete block design (RCBD)**: - Experimental units are grouped into homogeneous blocks (e.g., matching samples by processing date, run order, batch, or subject). - Within each block, experimental units are randomly assigned across the treatments. By ensuring that every treatment is represented within each block, differences between blocks can be mathematically factored out of the error variance when testing for treatment effects. ### Confounding When a design places only one treatment into each block (Panel B above), the treatment effect is entirely **confounded** with the block effect. Any observed difference between Treatment A and Treatment B could be attributable to the biological treatment or to the technical differences between Block 1 and Block 2. Unless one assumes that block effects are strictly zero—an untestable assumption in this design—valid statistical conclusions about the treatment cannot be drawn. ## Case Studies ### Mouse T-Cell Populations Duguet et al. (2017) evaluated regulatory T cells (Treg) versus conventional T cells (Tconv) in mice. Pools of Treg and Tconv cells were isolated by flow cytometry from individual biological replicates (mice). Consider two ways this data can be collected: 1. **Completely Randomized Design (CRD)**: 4 biological replicates are processed purely as Tconv and 4 separate biological replicates are processed as Treg (e.g., `peptidesCRD.txt`). Comparisons are conducted across independent subjects ($n = 4$ per group, 8 subjects total). 2. **Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD)**: 4 biological replicates (mice) are used, but from each individual mouse, both a Treg and a Tconv sample are extracted and profiled (e.g., `peptidesRCB.txt`). In the RCBD layout, each mouse serves as its own block. Pairwise differences between Treg and Tconv can be computed within the same animal: $$\Delta_i = y_{i, \text{Treg}} - y_{i, \text{Tconv}}$$ Because inter-individual mouse-to-mouse baseline variation is eliminated from $\Delta_i$, the residual variance is reduced to technical and intra-individual variation. Consequently, testing treatment differences in an RCB design generally yields substantially higher statistical power—and thus a greater number of discovered differentially abundant proteins—than a CRD with equivalent replicate numbers. ### Multi-Region Human Heart Proteome A dataset examining human cardiac tissue sampled four distinct anatomical regions from 3 human patients (identifiers 3, 4, and 8): - Left Atrium (LA) - Right Atrium (RA) - Left Ventricle (LV) - Right Ventricle (RV) Here, each patient acts as a block containing all four anatomical regions. #### Model Formulation To assess differences across the heart, the linear model for a protein's abundance includes: - A blocking factor for `Patient` (accounting for baseline biological variability across individuals 3, 4, and 8). - Factors for the anatomical conditions: chamber type (`Atrium` vs. `Ventricle`) and lateral position (`Left` vs. `Right`), or a single combined four-level factor representing heart region (`LA`, `RA`, `LV`, `RV`). #### Research Contrasts Using the four region parameters ($\mu_{\text{LA}}, \mu_{\text{RA}}, \mu_{\text{LV}}, \mu_{\text{RV}}$), specific scientific questions are evaluated using linear contrasts: 1. **Left ventricle versus left atrium**: $$L_1 = \mu_{\text{LV}} - \mu_{\text{LA}}$$ 2. **Right ventricle versus right atrium**: $$L_2 = \mu_{\text{RV}} - \mu_{\text{RA}}$$ 3. **Average ventricular versus average atrial proteome**: $$L_3 = \frac{\mu_{\text{LV}} + \mu_{\text{RV}}}{2} - \frac{\mu_{\text{LA}} + \mu_{\text{RA}}}{2}$$ 4. **Interaction (differential ventricular–atrial shift between left and right heart)**: $$L_4 = (\mu_{\text{LV}} - \mu_{\text{LA}}) - (\mu_{\text{RV}} - \mu_{\text{RA}})$$ Contrast $L_3$ evaluates global functional divergence between pump chambers (ventricles) and receiving chambers (atria). Because $L_3$ averages across both sides of the heart, it exploits twice as many observations per contrast estimate as $L_1$ or $L_2$, reducing standard errors and typically discovering a higher number of statistically significant proteins. Conversely, $L_4$ tests whether chamber-specific proteomic divergence depends on laterality, which represents an interaction term and inherently possesses lower statistical power than main-effect comparisons. ## Sources - **3.1 Basic Statistical Concepts**: Distinction between experimental units and observational units; biological repeats versus pseudo-replicates; definitions of blocking and randomized complete block designs; confounding mechanisms. - **3.2 Blocking: Mouse T-cell example**: Study design from Duguet et al. (2017) (PRIDE PXD004436); comparisons of CRD versus RCB data subsets; efficiency of within-block testing. - **3.3 Heart dataset**: Multi-region cardiac proteomics study across 3 patients (PRIDE PXD006675); formulation of anatomical factors, block terms, and linear contrasts ($L_1$ to $L_4$).
